newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong's securities watchdog hires China expert.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's securities watchdog hires China expert.

text.p: Hong Kong's securities and futures watchdog has strengthened its China advisory team in advance of the handover and in the wake of rampant red chip speculation, a commission spokesman said on Friday.
The Hong Kong Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has hired Li Qingyuan, a Beijing-trained economist who worked briefly at the China Securities Regulatory Commission, China's securities watchdog.
"Li Qingyuan has been hired as a policy advisor on issues related to China, including corporate finance," said William Weeks, senior manager in corporate communications at the SFC.
Li would be working with Laura Cha, executive director in charge of the corporate finance division, said Weeks.

Li has a doctorate in economics and worked for Goldman Sachs in Beijing, Weeks said, but could give no other details about Li's background, including her title or the date she would start working at the SFC.
Recent feverish speculation in red chips -- companies incorporated and listed in Hong Kong but backed by Chinese capital -- has alarmed both local authorities and those in Beijing.

Hong Kong investors, analysts and company officers have also expressed concern that some share prices have climbed too high, prompted by speculation of future injections of cheap assets by the parents into the Hong Kong listed companies.
Chinese authorities have also said domestic laws were unclear on the issue of red chips and asset injections by their mainland-based parent companies.
But the Chinese laws were generally believed not to have jurisdiction over these red chip companies.

SFC chairman Anthony Neoh met with China Securities Regulatory Commission officials in Beijing in mid-April to discuss the separate roles of the two securities watchdogs on issues related to red chip stock offerings.
The two organisations reached a consensus over a division of responsibility, Neoh said on April 16 at a securities conference in Beijing.
China would govern the upstream companies. Red chips, which were Hong Kong companies, would be handled according to the Basic Law, Beijing's mini-constitution for post-handover Hong Kong, Neoh said
He did not provide any details of the approval process for new listings of red chip companies in Hong Kong.
Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
